newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BOE says some of pound strength irrational.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BOE says some of pound strength irrational.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Wednesday that some of the pound's steady rise against other major currencies had been irrational.

Speaking to the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee, he also said that the Bank's new monetary policy committee, which the Labour government put in charge of interest rates in May, did not have a bias towards raising rates.
Asked about the strength of sterling, which has surged over 25 percent in the past year, the central bank chief replied:
"I can't explain why it's risen to the extent that it has and therefore I am bound to assume that some of it is irrational, erratic."
Commenting on the buoyancy of the London stock market, George said there might be some "irrational exuberance" but it was probably less extreme than in the United States.
Late last year, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan sent U.S. stock and bond markets spiralling lower by warning of "irrational exuberance" in the markets.

"The view from the stock market is very important. Of course we are aware of perceptions of 'irrational exuberance' which could have monetary effects," George said. "But if there is irrational exuberance here, it is probably a bit less than in the United States."

George said that if Britain was to join a single European currency, it would be unwise to do so anywhere near the pound's current level. Sterling touched 3.0878 deutschemarks on Wednesday, its highest level since September 1989.
"It's an impossible question to answer but if we were to join, it would be very unwise to do so at anything likely the rate we are at today," he said.

Official interest rates have been increased three times in as many months to their present 6.75 percent level and many economists expect the Bank to raise them again soon. Critics of Labour finance minister Gordon Brown's decision to give the central bank freedom to set interest rates argue that it will have a natural bias in favour of raising rates to combat inflation, possibly to the detriment of economic growth.
George insisted this was not the case.
"Why would the committee not be biased one way or the other? Basically, because its instruction is a totally symmetrical one," he told the Treasury Select Committee.
The government has set a target for underlying inflation of 2.5 percent, but the Bank is obliged to provide a public explanation if inflation is one percentage point above or below the target.

Asked by opposition Conservative members of the committee if he agreed that the government had failed to do enough to dampen personal consumption in the July 2 budget, George said the budget had reinforced a fiscal tightening already put in place by the previous government.
"I think that certainly goes in the right direction -- I would say it goes quite a long way in the right direction," he said.
